Question centrale : pourquoi certaines entreprises réussissent-elles mieux que d'autres ?
Rumelt : diagnostic → guiding policy → actions cohérentes (ex. Southwest Airlines).
Mauvaise stratégie : ne pas affronter le problème, confondre objectifs et stratégie, mauvais objectifs, fluff.
Vision (pourquoi, C-level) → stratégie (quoi, top management) → tactique (comment, terrain).
Changer les règles du jeu : Apple (océan bleu), Azincourt, Kennedy et la Lune.
ext
Analyse externe : les choix sont à la firme, le contexte non. Trois couches : macro (PESTEL), industrie (5 forces), firme.
Quatre canaux vers le profit : demande, coûts, concurrence, règles.
PESTEL : prioriser par impact × prévisibilité (planifier, scénarios, surveiller, mettre de côté).
Cinq forces : entrants, fournisseurs, clients, substituts, rivalité ; plus elles sont fortes, moins l'industrie est profitable.
SWOT : interne (forces, faiblesses) vs externe (opportunités, menaces, issues du PESTEL et des 5 forces) ; utile seulement s'il finit en choix.
Uber : clients et rivalité forts → industrie peu attractive ; profit par l'échelle et l'écosystème ; option F+O : plateforme de demande des robotaxis.
Cas aérien : low cost (un seul avion, point-à-point, rotations rapides) = 47 ans de profit Southwest ; Covid : trafic -90 %, la résilience est un choix (cash, flexibilité, options).
Stratégie intentionnelle → réalisée et émergente (leviers : structure, systèmes, personnes).
int
Analyse externe : où est le profit ? Analyse interne : qui peut le capter ? Les effets propres au business comptent plus que l’industrie dans les données citées.
Ressources (ce que la firme possède) → capacités (ce qu’elle sait faire) → avantage concurrentiel.
VRIO : Valuable, Rare, Imperfectly imitable, Organized to exploit. Parité ≠ avantage temporaire ≠ avantage durable ; sans O, avantage inexploité.
Imitation freinée par l’histoire, l’ambiguïté causale et la complexité sociale. Les capacités dynamiques permettent de détecter, saisir et reconfigurer.
Chaîne de valeur : activités principales et de soutien ; Zara et Southwest gagnent par un système d’activités qui se renforcent.
Choisir sa place : intégration amont/aval, spécialisation, contrôle d’un goulot. Les marges des acteurs de la chaîne ne sont pas directement comparables.
Conseil : six familles ; organisation industrie × fonction × géographie ; modèle pyramidal. Chiffres d’effectifs/salaires approximatifs, datés et à périmètres différents.
Due diligence commerciale = marché/position (S2), opérationnelle = ressources/capacités (S3), complétées par les experts financiers, juridiques et techniques.
bls
Stratégie métier = 3 choix : qui (quels clients servir), quoi (quels besoins, quelle promesse), comment (quelles ressources et activités). Choisir, c'est aussi renoncer.
Avantage concurrentiel : créer plus de valeur que les rivaux, telle que le client la perçoit. WTP 100 €, prix 70 €, coût 50 € → surplus client 30 €, marge 20 €.

Deux leviers : baisser le coût (plus de marge ou prix plus bas à marge égale) ou augmenter la disposition à payer (différenciation). L'avantage n'existe que si les clients le voient (Bezos : le client est un invité, nous sommes l'hôte).

Porter : 2 sources d'avantage (coût, différenciation) × 2 périmètres (marché large, segment étroit) = leadership coût (Ryanair, Lidl), différenciation (Apple, Zara), focalisation coût (Dacia, hotelF1), focalisation différenciation (Hermès, Ferrari).
Leadership coût : coût le plus bas pour un produit acceptable, prix au niveau du marché — low cost n'est pas low price. Sources : échelle, apprentissage, simplicité, intrants bon marché.
Différenciation : le test est que la prime payée par le client dépasse le coût de la différence (Hermès : savoir-faire et rareté ; Zara : vitesse).

Focalisation : mieux servir un segment (risque : niche trop petite) ; hybride (IKEA, Toyota) : plus de valeur à coût modéré, possible avec un système solide malgré l'avertissement « stuck in the middle » de Porter.

Fit (Porter 1996) : une position = un système d'activités cohérentes + des trade-offs (Ryanair : un seul avion, aéroports secondaires, rotations rapides, pas de correspondances). Sans trade-offs, pas de position.
Chaque stratégie répond différemment aux 5 forces : le coût protège des guerres de prix et des acheteurs puissants ; la différenciation fidélise et rend les offres incomparables.

Cycle de l'avantage : construire → exploiter → imiter → éroder → renouveler. Érosion par imitation, technologie, entrants par le bas, goûts. Réponses : défendre, étendre, renouveler. Les avantages prix s'érodent vite, ceux fondés sur la culture lentement.

Fil mode : quatre firmes, une garde-robe — marge opérationnelle Hermès 41 %, Inditex ≈20 %, H&M 8 %, Shein ≈4 % (dernier exercice complet ; Hermès, H&M, Shein 2025, Inditex exercice 2024). Chaque marge reflète un choix de position.

Lecture des positions : Primark et Ryanair = leadership coût ; Hermès = focalisation différenciation ; Apple = différenciation ; Zara et IKEA = hybrides ; Shein = coût + vitesse ; H&M = position à débattre (moins cher que Zara ? plus mode que Primark ?).

Pourquoi les clients choisissent : deux leviers seulement — payer moins (prix bas, sans fioritures) ou obtenir plus (qualité, design, marque, vitesse, confiance). Le coût joue sur le premier, la différenciation sur le second.
Nouvel espace de marché (« blue ocean ») : rendre la concurrence non pertinente (Cirque du Soleil : théâtre + cirque) — difficile à répéter, facile à imiter une fois prouvé.
plt

Méthode de lecture en 4 questions : quel coût/barrière tombe (5 forces) → où est la valeur durable (VRIN) → quelle décision est forcée (rivaux) → quel risque/arbitrage. On change d'objet, pas de méthode.

Schumpeter (1942) : destruction créatrice — l'innovation remplace l'ancienne économie, elle ne s'y ajoute pas. Christensen (1997) : disruption par le bas — une offre simple et moins chère gagne le bas du marché puis remonte. Souvent les deux (Amazon a commencé par les livres).
Internet : 4 coûts tombés à (presque) zéro — chercher, copier, distribuer, apparier (Goldfarb & Tucker, 2019) → entrée facile, intermédiaires dépossédés de leur rôle payé.
Coût marginal quasi nul : le coût fixe est la barrière ; l'échelle paie (le plus gros peut pricer le plus bas) ; le gratuit devient possible si un second payeur existe (annonceurs, autre côté).
Longue traîne (Anderson 2004) : les niches additionnées peuvent rivaliser avec les hits ; nuance Elberse (2008) : les hits portent encore une large part du revenu.
Pipeline (Zara) vend, plateforme (Vinted) connecte : elle possède la connexion entre les deux côtés, ni l'article ni la vente. La plupart des firmes sont hybrides (Zalando).
4 effets de réseau : direct (messagerie), croisé (Airbnb hôtes/voyageurs), négatif (spam, congestion), local (VTC par ville). Ils relèvent la barrière à l'entrée mais chacun a sa limite.
Poule-et-œuf d'un marché biface : amorcer un côté, subventionner, viser local, faire ce qui ne scale pas (Airbnb NY 2009 : photos porte-à-porte, revenu ×2).
Qui paie = choix stratégique : on monétise le côté qui valorise le plus la transaction (Vinted : acheteurs paient, vendeurs gratuits) ; cela détermine quel côté on attire d'abord.
4 risques de plateforme : leakage (traiter en dehors), qualité/modération (coût central), régulation (DMA 2022/1925 applicable depuis 2023, séance 7), dépendance aux règles d'un seul acteur.

Modèles : gratuit financé par la pub (Amazon ads 68,6 Mds$ en 2025, lancé 2012) ; vendre le résultat pas le produit (Rolls-Royce Power-by-the-Hour, 1962) ; abonnement = creux de revenu initial, ne paie que si les clients restent (Adobe : revenu −7,9 % en 2013 pendant que l'abonnement +69 %).
SaaS : ARR = MRR × 12 ; NRR > 100 % = croissance sans nouveau client ; churn = pertes qui coûtent des années ; Rule of 40 = croissance + marge (30 % + 15 % = 45).
Amazon 2025 : AWS = 18 % des ventes nettes (716,9 Mds$) mais 57 % du résultat opérationnel (80 Mds$) — l'activité la plus visible n'est pas le moteur de profit ; la stratégie est le portefeuille.
ma
Stratégie d'entreprise (corporate) : dans quels métiers être, quelles étapes de la chaîne de valeur, quels pays — la M&A déplace une frontière, et céder une activité est aussi un choix stratégique.
Une acquisition est une action, pas une stratégie (Rumelt) : à chaque deal, demander à quel diagnostic il répond et pourquoi acheter plutôt que construire (build) ou s'allier (borrow).

5 raisons d'acheter reliées aux outils du cours : échelle → 5 forces (Vusion-Pricer) ; contrôle d'une étape → chaîne de valeur (Amazon-Whole Foods) ; capacité → VRIO (Facebook-Instagram, Vusion-Memory) ; entrer sur un marché → barrières à l'entrée (Walmart-Jet.com) ; se transformer → corporate (Microsoft-Nokia, échec).

Build : contrôle total et sa culture, mais lent (à choisir si on a les compétences et le temps). Borrow : vitesse et risque partagé, mais dépendance (si un accès suffit). Buy : vitesse + contrôle, mais prime et risque d'intégration (si le contrôle est nécessaire et l'intégration possible). Capron & Mitchell (2012).
Organique vs acquisition : l'organique coûte sans prime mais prend des années ; l'acquisition apporte clients, équipe et savoir-faire d'un coup au prix d'une prime et d'une fusion de cultures.
Taux d'échec des M&A cité : 70–90 % (Christensen et al., HBR 2011) ; 12 cents perdus par dollar dépensé à l'annonce (1998–2001, Moeller et al.). Le vendeur capte généralement la prime.
Valeur pour l'acheteur = synergies − prime − coûts d'intégration. Synergies de coûts souvent livrées, synergies de revenus souvent décevantes ; malédiction du gagnant dans les enchères.

Facteurs d'échec : surpayer, synergies surestimées, choc de cultures, intégration lente, distraction du cœur, régulateurs ignorés. Les échecs se jouent avant la signature ou dans les 100 premiers jours.
Acheteur stratégique (synergies, paie en cash ou actions, peut payer plus) vs acheteur financier (rendement puis revente, cash souvent avec dette, fondateurs souvent maintenus).

3 méthodes de valorisation : comparables (multiple × métrique, dépend du marché), transactions précédentes (incluent la prime de contrôle, ex. Pricer +29,6 %), DCF (sensible aux hypothèses). VE − dette nette = valeur des capitaux propres. Prix maximal = valeur autonome + synergies réellement capturables.
Cession en 6 étapes : préparer → approcher → premières offres → due diligence → signing → closing. Dual track : cession et levée en parallèle pour tester le prix et garder un repli.
Le prix, c'est aussi les conditions : earn-out et garanties (non coté), prime et fairness opinion (coté), carve-out, LBO, fusion en actions (qui contrôle ?).

Après le closing : préparer → rassurer (jour 1) → organiser (100 jours) → intégrer (ans 1–3). Degrés d'intégration (Haspeslagh & Jemison) : absorption, symbiose, holding, préservation, selon besoin de partage des ressources × besoin d'autonomie.

Les M&A suivent le coût de l'argent : record 2021 (6,8 T$), creux 2022–23, mégadeals record en 2025 (68 deals > 10 Mds $). En 2024 les acheteurs cherchaient des économies (59 % scale), en 2025 de la croissance et des capacités (60 % scope) — Bain.
mem
Cas Memory : logiciel + experts qui transforment les données de vente des retailers en décisions (assortiment, prix, promos) ; fondée en 2018, rentable (52 % EBITDA), jamais financée.
Diagnostic : marché français gagné, dépendance à 3 retailers (97 % du revenu, propriétaires des données), mi-logiciel mi-services, pas de réseau à l'étranger → ne peut pas grandir seule.

Guiding policy : s'appuyer sur un partenaire plus grand pour devenir un acteur mondial logiciel + donnée, en restant neutre entre retailers (exclut : retailer partenaire, expansion seule, sur-mesure).
Dual track fonds + corporates : la concurrence fixe le prix et protège du désistement ; Carrefour écarté pour préserver la neutralité (= la valeur).
Vusion choisi à prix égal (80 M€) : certitude, 100 % cash au closing, plan et personnes ; les synergies commerciales ont déçu (les synergies de revenus sont les plus dures).
Un maximum n'est pas un paiement : 80 M€ perçus au closing + earn-out 5+3+1 M€ ; le « super bonus » jusqu'à 50 M€ est resté hors d'atteinte.

Why does ride-hailing illustrate a LOCAL network effect?
The value stays within a city: you need drivers nearby
Dominating Paris is useless in Lyon; each network-effect kind has its own limit.
Airbnb, New York, 2009 (founders photographing listings themselves) illustrates which launch tactic?
Manual work to get the first users; reported result: New York revenue ×2. The 4 tactics: seed one side, subsidise, go local, do what does not scale.
On Vinted, sellers pay nothing and buyers pay a protection fee. What is the logic?
The platform charges the side that values the transaction most and keeps the other free
Who pays is a strategic choice (media: readers free, advertisers pay; cards: merchants pay).
The two sides meet on the platform, then deal outside it to avoid fees
Other risks: quality (moderation cost), regulation (DMA), dependence on one owner's rules.
Bans platforms over one million users
Applicable since 2023, it regulates large platforms that have become gatekeepers
Regulation follows market power; covered in session 7.
Amazon 2025: AWS is 18% of net sales. What share of operating income?
The most visible business is not the main profit engine — strategy is the portfolio, not the label.
A loop where each turn eases the next (low prices → customers → sellers → volume → low costs → low prices)
Self-reinforcing growth; class question: which link is hardest to copy?
An NRR (net revenue retention) of 110% means…
The existing customer base generates 10% more revenue than a year ago — growth with no new customer
NRR counts upsell and cancellations; ARR = MRR × 12; Rule of 40 = growth + margin.
A SaaS firm shows 30% growth and 15% margin. What does the Rule of 40 say?
Rule of thumb balancing growth and profitability.
Adobe, fiscal 2013: total revenue $4.06bn (−7.9%) but subscriptions +69%. What is the lesson?
Switching to subscriptions creates a revenue dip before the recurring base builds
Avoid running both models at once
The switch costs revenue first; it pays back only if customers stay.
Rolls-Royce 'Power-by-the-Hour' (1962): why does this model align incentives?
The maker earns more when the engine flies (not when it breaks): you sell the outcome, made measurable by monitoring
Before: sell the engine, then the repairs. After: a fixed price per flying hour.
An action that must answer a diagnosis
'Grow through acquisitions' is not a strategy.
Amazon buys Whole Foods ($13.7bn, 2017). Which reason, and which course tool?
Control a stage of the chain → value chain
Controlling a stage of the value chain.
Walmart buys Jet.com ($3.3bn, 2016) rather than building. Why buy?
The premium is smaller than the build cost
Speed: clients, team and know-how at once
Acquiring is fast but costs a premium and merges two cultures.
In the build / borrow / buy frame, the Microsoft–OpenAI alliance ($1bn + cloud partnership, 2019) is…
You have the skills and the time
The asset is rare and impossible to copy
Borrow = contracts, licences, alliances: speed and shared cost, but dependence.
Synergies must exceed the premium AND integration costs.
Cross-selling requires selling differently; cost savings deliver more easily.
In an auction, the 'winner's curse' means…
The winner is always sued by regulators
The winner is often the bidder who most overestimated the target
The winner must pay in shares
Hence price discipline: be ready to walk away.
The M&A failure rate quoted in the course:
Buying is easy; creating value is hard. The seller usually captures the premium.
The maximum a buyer should pay for a target:
Its stand-alone value + the synergies it can really capture
Beyond that, the deal destroys value for the buyer.
Enterprise value €500m, net debt €80m. What do shareholders receive?
Which valuation method includes a control premium by construction?
E.g. Vusion offered +29.6% over Pricer's last price.
Small changes in assumptions change the value a lot
Growth, margins, investment, discount rate: all assumptions.
A premium paid upfront to the seller
Part of the price paid later if the plan is met
A bank guarantee from the buyer
Typical of unlisted firms: cash at closing + milestones; the seller bears part of the risk.
Running a sale and a fundraising (or IPO) in parallel
Buyers compete, the price is tested, and you keep a fallback.
Correct order of the six steps of a sale:
Approach → prepare → due diligence → first offers → signing → closing
Prepare → approach → first offers → due diligence → signing → closing
Prepare → first offers → approach → due diligence → closing → signing
Approach → first offers → prepare → signing → due diligence → closing
Instagram left largely autonomous inside Facebook after 2012: which integration mode?
Little to share + high need for autonomy = preserve the target.
A financial buyer (private-equity fund) is distinctive because…
It always pays more thanks to synergies
It seeks a return, then a resale in a few years
It always integrates the target into its group
Cash, often with debt; founders often stay in charge.
In 2025, most large deals (> $1bn) were motivated by…
Scope: growth, new countries, new capabilities
Memory (2022): what share of revenue comes from its three largest retail groups?
Intermarché 67% (France + international), Carrefour 24%, Auchan 5% — and these groups own the data Memory works on.
Why is Memory's bargaining power over its clients weak?
Three retail groups bring 97% of revenue and own the data — they can build in-house
Buyer power (S2): concentration + ownership of the key input.
The case's diagnosis, in one sentence:
Memory must cut costs to stay profitable
Memory has won its home market, but depends on a few powerful retailers, is half software half services, and has no network abroad: it cannot take the next step alone
Memory should sell to Carrefour before competitors do
A diagnosis names the critical challenge; each part maps to a course tool (S2 buyers, S3 VRIO, S5 model, S6 entry).
Go deep in France, alone, financed by profits
Sell mainly to brands, in direct
Lean on a bigger partner to become a global software and data player, while staying neutral between retailers
Hire twenty salespeople and open offices abroad
It answers every part of the diagnosis and rules out: a retailer as partner, going abroad alone, more custom projects.
'Become the reference in data for the whole retail industry globally' is…
An ambition, not a policy: it says where, not how
A guiding policy says what will and will not be done; a goal gives no approach.
Why was Carrefour refused as a bidder for Memory?
Other retailers would not keep a data supplier owned by their rival — neutrality was part of Memory's value
A buyer can destroy the value it buys.
Why run a dual track (funds + corporates) in September 2022?
Competition between buyers sets the price, and a fallback protects against another walk-away
Because one track is illegal in France
A growth fund had walked away the day before closing in July 2022.
The three 2022-2023 offers valued Memory at the same €80m. What made the difference?
Certainty, structure and the buyer's plan (100% cash at closing, store data, global reach)
Vusion signed in Feb 2023: 100% cash at closing + earn-out + free shares, and it answered the diagnosis.
Why did the growth fund walk away in July 2022?
The ECB raised rates for the first time since 2011 and the Nasdaq ended 2022 down 33% — investors stopped paying for growth alone
Memory lost Carrefour as a client
M&A follows the cost of money (S6).
After the deal, what disappointed most?
The integration of data and teams
Commercial (revenue) synergies — very different businesses, sales teams used to selling hardware
Revenue synergies are the hardest to deliver: the theory said so, the case confirms it.
'A maximum is not a payment' refers to…
The headline value (earn-out on the plan, super bonus up to €50m) versus what was actually received
Received: €80m at closing + €5m+€3m+€1m earn-out; the super bonus stayed out of reach. Read deal announcements with care.
In the funds' bear case on Memory, which risk is NOT cited?
A one-man show: everything rests on the founders
Valued like IT services, not software
A churn problem on core clients
Churn was zero on core clients — that is the bull case. The bear case adds retailer power (revenue + data).

Why strategy?

  • Central question: why do some companies perform better than others? The answer lies in their choices, not their size or industry.
  • Strategic decision: medium/long-term orientation, aims at a competitive advantage, commits resources, considers Company–Customer–Competition.

Good strategy: the kernel (3 steps)

  • Diagnosis: the real problem, not the symptoms.
  • Guiding policy: the chosen angle of attack (it rules out other angles).
  • Coherent actions: concrete, coordinated steps that reinforce each other.
  • Southwest Airlines: diagnosis = customers want cheap point-to-point flights, short trips are time-sensitive → policy = lowest-cost airline on short routes → actions = one aircraft type (737), 15-minute turnarounds, no assigned seats, secondary airports. Every action reinforces the same goal.

Bad strategy: 4 signs

  • Fluff: buzzwords without direction ("customer-centric intermediation").
  • Failure to face the problem: objectives instead of a diagnosis.
  • Mistaking goals for strategy: "+20%" is a wish, not a plan.
  • Bad strategic objectives: wish lists disconnected from the challenge (47 strategies, 178 actions).
  • Test a strategy: does it confront the real challenge? Is there a guiding policy, not just goals? Are actions coordinated? Can you explain why each choice matters?

Vision, strategy, tactics

VisionStrategyTactics
QuestionWhyWhatHow
OwnerC-levelTop managementField managers
  • Mission = the current offer, who we are · vision = where we are going.
  • Building a strategy: framing (vision, mission) → analysis (external: PESTEL, 5 forces; internal: resources, value chain) → presentation → organisation, with feedback loops.
  • Changing the game: create a blue ocean rather than fight in the red one; redefine the game so your strengths become decisive (Apple: simplicity and design vs IBM's specs; the Moon bet: a race decided by industrial resources the Soviets lacked).

Why start outside

  • The choices are yours (what to offer, to whom, how); the context is not. A position only exists relative to customers, rivals and rules.
  • Three layers: macro-environment → industry → your firm. Four channels from the outside to your profit: demand, costs, competition, rules.

PESTEL (macro)

  • Political · Economic · Social · Technological · Environmental · Legal.
  • Sort each factor in the impact × predictability matrix: high + predictable → plan; high + uncertain → scenarios; low + predictable → monitor; low + uncertain → set aside.

Porter's Five Forces (industry)

The stronger the forces, the lower the industry's profit potential.

ForceStrong when…Example
New entrantsCheap entry, weak brands, easy distributionOnline fashion brands
SuppliersFew suppliers, no substitute inputs, costly switchingChip makers → carmakers
BuyersFew large buyers, look-alike products, easy switchingSupermarkets vs food brands
SubstitutesA different product meets the same needStreaming vs cinema
RivalryMany equal players, slow growth, high fixed costs, little differentiationTelecom operators

Application: Uber

  • Buyers high (switch apps in seconds) · rivalry high (Lyft, Bolt, DiDi price war) · suppliers medium (drivers multi-home; bonuses keep supply) · entrants medium (network effects deter; robotaxis could enter) · substitutes medium (car, transit, bikes).
  • Takeaway: unattractive industry; Uber profits from scale and ecosystem (Rides, Eats, Uber One). S+O option: become the demand platform for robotaxi fleets.

SWOT (the firm in its context)

  • Strengths/weaknesses = internal (you control them); opportunities/threats = external (from PESTEL and the five forces).
  • Four combos: S+O attack · W+O fix a gap · S+T defend · W+T reduce exposure. A SWOT only matters if it ends in choices.

Airline case: lessons

  • 2019 diagnosis (Airbus-Boeing duopoly, price-sensitive customers, high fixed costs, substitutes on short routes) → the five forces pointed to low cost: one aircraft type, point-to-point, fast turnarounds, no frills (Southwest, Ryanair).
  • March 2020: no analysis removes outside shocks. Resilience is a strategic choice: cash, flexibility and options decide who comes out ahead.

From the industry to the firm

  • External analysis shows where profit is; internal analysis asks who can capture it. Same shocks, different outcomes (Southwest profitable 1973–2019 while rivals went bankrupt).
  • Business-specific effects explain 32% of profitability variance vs 19% for industry: what happens inside the firm matters most.

Resources → capabilities → advantage

  • Resources = what the firm owns (assets, brands, people, data); capabilities = what it can do with them (routines, organisation). Resources alone do not win.
  • Tangible: cash, plants, fleets. Intangible: brand, reputation, know-how, culture, data — often more durable, but fragile and hard to measure.

VRIO: four tests

  • Valuable (exploits an opportunity / neutralises a threat) · Rare · Inimitable (costly to copy) · Organised to exploit.
  • Not V → disadvantage · V only → parity · V+R → temporary advantage · V+R+I+O → sustained advantage. Without O, the advantage stays unused (Xerox PARC).

Barriers to imitation

  • History (built over years: Hermès) · causal ambiguity (even insiders cannot isolate what works: Apple design) · social complexity (culture, trust: Southwest, Toyota).

Advantage erodes: rigidities and dynamic capabilities

  • Strengths become rigidities: Kodak protected film (bankruptcy 2012); Nokia's hardware did not transfer to software. Southwest's operating margin fell from 20% (2015) to 1.5% (2025) as rivals copied.
  • Dynamic capabilities: sense change, seize it, reshape resources (Fujifilm → health care). VRIO is a snapshot — ask how long a resource stays valuable.

Value chain and activity systems

  • Primary: inbound logistics → operations → outbound → marketing & sales → service. Support: infrastructure, HR, technology, procurement.
  • The advantage is the system, not one activity: Zara's store → design → factory → store loop; Southwest's mutually reinforcing activities. Continental Lite copied pieces and kept its hubs — it failed; Ryanair rebuilt the whole system.

Where to play in the industry chain

  • Margins differ by stage (smartphones, FY2025: TSMC 51%, Apple 32%, Samsung MX 10%, Foxconn 3%). Pick your stage: backward integration (Netflix content), forward integration (Apple stores), specialise (TSMC), or own the bottleneck (ASML).

Due diligence combines both toolboxes

CheckQuestion
Commercial (S2)Market attractiveness and target's position?
Operational (S3)Does the target have the resources and capabilities it claims?
FinancialReliable accounts? Right price?
LegalContracts, risks, obligations?
TechnicalCode and technology review?

Business-level strategy: three choices

  • Who: which customers we serve (and which we leave) · What: which needs we meet · How: which resources and activities deliver the promise. Choosing also means not serving.
  • Levels: corporate (which businesses) → business (how to win in one) → functional (how to execute).

Competitive advantage: more value than rivals

QuantityDefinitionExample
Willingness to pay (WTP)The most the customer would pay€100
PriceWhat the customer actually pays€70
CostWhat producing costs the firm€50
Customer surplusWTP − price (why they buy from you)€30
MarginPrice − cost€20
  • Only two levers: lower cost or raise WTP. Supply-side view starts from resources (R, I, O); demand-side view starts from what customers value (V). A resource without a customer who cares has no value.

Porter's generic strategies

Broad marketNarrow segment
Lower costCost leadership — Ryanair, Walmart, LidlCost focus — Basic-Fit, Dacia
DifferentiationDifferentiation — Apple, NikeDifferentiation focus — Hermès, Ferrari

Cost leadership

  • Lowest cost for an acceptable product; price at or slightly below market. Low cost is not low price.
  • Sources: scale and learning, simple design, cheap inputs. Benefits: profit through price wars; scale as a barrier. Risks: an even lower-cost model, new technology, losing sight of what customers value.

Differentiation

  • Something customers see as unique; the test: the premium must exceed the cost of the difference.
  • Sources: quality, brand, design, speed (Hermès, Apple, Zara). Benefits: premium, loyalty, less price pressure. Risks: premium above perceived value, "good enough" imitators, changing tastes.

Focus, hybrid, blue ocean

  • Focus: serve one segment better than broad rivals (risk: niche too small). Hybrid: more value at moderate cost — IKEA, Zara; works with a strong system. Without trade-offs, "cost and quality" = stuck in the middle (H&M).
  • Blue ocean: make competition irrelevant (Cirque du Soleil); easy to imitate once proven.

Fit: a position is a system of activities

  • Ryanair: one aircraft type + secondary airports + fast turnarounds + no frills + online sales — each activity serves the position, and trade-offs (no connections, no business class) protect it.

Dynamics: no advantage lasts

  • Cycle: build → exploit → imitate → erode → renew. Erosion forces: imitation, technology, entrants from below, changing tastes.
  • Respond: defend (raise barriers), extend (new customers/markets), renew (build the next advantage first). Culture- and know-how-based advantages fade slowly; price-based ones fade fast.

Reading method: technology as strategy (4 questions)

  • 1. Cost: what cost or barrier falls, and who enters? 2. Value: where is durable value? 3. Decision: which decision does it force on rivals? 4. Risk: which risk or trade-off?
  • A technology is not a strategic fact until it moves a position; the tools of sessions 1–4 apply as they are.

Creative destruction and disruption

  • Replacement (Schumpeter): new combinations of technology and business model replace the old economy.
  • From below (Christensen): a cheaper, simpler offer wins the low end, then moves up (Amazon started with books).

Four costs fell to (almost) zero

CostBeforeNow
SearchingTravel agency, printed directorySearch engines, booking sites
CopyingPrinted encyclopaediaWikipedia
DistributingA CD in a shopA stream
MatchingClassified adsOnline marketplaces
  • Average cost = fixed ÷ units + marginal. Near-zero marginal cost → scale pays more (the largest can price lowest) and free becomes possible (a second side pays: advertisers).
  • Long tail: niches add up (Anderson) — but hits still carry much of the revenue (Elberse): check before you bet.

Pipeline vs platform

  • Pipeline (Zara): designs, makes, ships, sells — value flows one way. Platform (Vinted): owns the connection between two sides, neither the item nor the sale. Most firms are hybrids (Zalando).
  • Anatomy: side A gains reach/payment/trust · the platform sets the rules (matching, payment, moderation) · side B gains choice/price/protection.

Network effects: four kinds

KindMechanismExample
DirectMore users → better for every userMessaging
Cross-sideMore hosts → more guests, and backAirbnb
NegativeCongestion, spam, fake reviewsReview platforms
LocalValue stays within one areaRide-hailing
  • Chicken-and-egg: seed one side, subsidise, go local, do what does not scale (Airbnb's founders photographing listings, New York 2009 → revenue ×2).
  • Who pays: charge the side that values the transaction most, keep the other free (Vinted: sellers free, buyers pay; media: readers free, advertisers pay).
  • Risks: leakage (deals move off-platform), quality (moderation becomes a core cost), regulation (DMA, gatekeepers), dependence on one owner's rules.

Flywheel, cloud, subscriptions

  • Flywheel (Amazon): low prices → customers → sellers → volume → lower costs → lower prices; each turn eases the next.
  • Amazon 2025: AWS = 18% of net sales but 57% of operating income — the most visible business is not the profit engine.
  • Subscription economics: ARR = MRR × 12 · NRR above 100% = growth with no new customer · churn costs future years · Rule of 40 = growth + margin ≥ 40. Switching from licence creates a revenue dip first (Adobe 2013: revenue −7.9%, subscriptions +69%).
  • Outcome selling: Rolls-Royce "Power-by-the-Hour" — sell flying hours, not engines; the maker earns more when the engine keeps flying (monitoring makes outcomes measurable).

From business to corporate strategy

  • Corporate strategy = which businesses to be in (products, vertical stages, geography); M&A moves a boundary — so does divesting.
  • Five ways to react when the market moves: defend, transform, buy, partner, ignore.
  • An acquisition is an action, not a strategy: ask which diagnosis it answers, and why buy rather than build or partner.

Five reasons to buy (mapped to course tools)

ReasonToolExample
Scale (buy a rival)Five ForcesVusion → Pricer (2026)
Control a stage of the chainValue chainAmazon → Whole Foods (2017)
Buy a capabilityVRIOFacebook → Instagram (2012)
Enter a marketEntry barriersWalmart → Jet.com (2016)
Diversify / transformCorporate strategyMicrosoft → Nokia phones (failed)

Build, borrow or buy

BuildBorrowBuy
GivesControl, own cultureSpeed, shared cost/riskSpeed + control
CostsTime, risk of being lateDependence on partnerPremium + integration risk
Use whenSkills + time availableNeed access, not ownershipNeed control, can integrate
  • Ask in order: can we build it? Can we borrow it? Only then: should we buy — and can we integrate?
  • M&A comes in waves (record $6.8tn in 2021 → $5.1tn in 2025): it follows the cost of money. Size guarantees nothing: 3 of the 10 biggest deals were later split or undone.

Value creation: synergies must exceed the premium

  • Value for the buyer = synergies − premium − integration costs.
  • Cost synergies often deliver; revenue synergies often disappoint. In an auction, the winner's curse: the winner is often the bidder who overestimated most. Quoted failure rate: 70–90%; the seller usually captures the premium.

Three ways to value a target

  • Comparable companies (multiple × metric; depends on market mood) · precedent transactions (include a control premium; few comparable deals) · DCF (intrinsic, but small assumption changes → big value changes).
  • Enterprise value − net debt = equity value. Max price = stand-alone value + the synergies you can really capture. Multiples move over time: SaaS EV/revenue 19.3x (2020) → 3.2x (2026).

Six steps of a sale

1. Prepare2. Approach3. First offers4. Due diligence5. Signing6. Closing
Adviser, memo, data roomTeaser, NDANon-binding, short listCommercial, financial, legal, techBinding offer, SPAShares and cash change hands
  • Dual track: run sale and fundraising/IPO in parallel — buyers compete, you keep a fallback. Earn-out: part of the price paid later if the plan is met.

After the deal: integration decides

  • Strategic buyer (synergies, can pay more) vs financial buyer (return, then resale in a few years; often debt-financed).
  • Integration modes (autonomy × resource-sharing): absorption (merge everything) · symbiosis (share resources, keep what makes the target special) · holding (financial control only) · preservation (leave it alone: Instagram in Facebook). Integrate too much and you kill what you bought; too little and synergies never come.

The case: Memory in 2022

  • Software + experts turning retailers' sales data into decisions (assortment, prices, promotions); brands pay to see their sales at each retailer. Founded Nov 2018, no outside money: €11.1m revenue (+76%), 52% EBITDA, 61 people.
  • Two-sided model, but the retailer owns the data: retailers pay a licence; brands pay via the retailer (45-55% revenue share) or in direct. 84% subscriptions, >95% gross margin, zero churn, 400+ brands.
  • Three retail groups = 97% of revenue (Intermarché 67%, Carrefour 24%, Auchan 5%). Rivals: NielsenIQ/IRI (Circana), in-house (Carrefour Links, dunnhumby), consulting, start-ups. Plan: ×6 by 2026 (€66.8m, 37 retailers, 24 abroad) — but every sale runs through the founders.

Step 1 — Diagnosis (the kernel again)

  • Strengths: fast profitable growth, trusted by French retail (NPS 45, zero churn), deep retail know-how, own technology, brands' revenue ×4 in 2022.
  • Caps: home market won · no network abroad · half software, half services (valued like services) · little power over retailers (97% of revenue + they own the data) · founder-led.
  • "Memory has won its home market, but it depends on a few powerful retailers, looks half software and half services, and has no network abroad: it cannot take the next step alone."

Step 2 — Guiding policy

  • Not a goal (says where, not how), not an action. A policy chooses and rules out. Three candidates: A · go deep at home alone · B · sell mainly to brands · C · team up to become the neutral bridge.
  • Chosen: lean on a bigger partner to become a global software and data player, while staying neutral between retailers. Rules out: a retailer as partner ✕ · going abroad alone ✕ · more custom projects ✕.

Step 3 — Coherent actions → team up

  • Most actions need someone else's network, data or money (product-ize custom work, win retailers abroad, sell without the founders). Four needs: defend (retailers building in-house), add value (more data), new offers (retail media), go international.
  • Four options: stay alone · raise from a fund (minority) · sell to a fund · sell to a strategic buyer. First choice: raise from a fund.

The sale process

  • Investors: bull case (rare profile, locked-in clients, platform ready to scale) vs bear case (one-man show, services not software, no international proof, retailer power) → funds wanted protection: earn-out, lock-in, warranties, vetoes.
  • July 2022: a growth fund offers €80m (40% cash-out + €5m cash-in, buy-and-build) — and walks away the day before closing (ECB's first rate hike since 2011; Nasdaq −33% in 2022: no more paying for growth alone).
  • Sept 2022: dual track (funds + corporates: Circana, Vusion) — competition sets the price, the fallback protects. Carrefour refused as a bidder: other retailers would not keep a data supplier owned by their rival — neutrality was part of the value.
  • Same €80m price, three structures: PE fund (40% at closing; walked away) · Circana (60% cash + milestones; not chosen) · Vusion (100% cash at closing + earn-out + free shares; signed Feb 2023). Certainty, structure, plan and people made the difference — not price.

After the deal (2023-2026) and lessons

  • Delivered: product, data and teams integrated (Memory → Vusion Intelligence). Below plan: commercial synergies — revenue synergies are the hardest to deliver; the case confirms the theory.
  • Five lessons: know why you sell (start from the diagnosis, not the price) · keep an alternative (until closing, nothing is done) · make buyers compete (dual track) · compare structures, not headlines · choose the plan and the people.
  • A maximum is not a payment: received €80m cash at closing + €5+3+1m earn-out; the "up to €50m" super bonus stayed out of reach — headlines read "well over €100m".
